subject: English
q: I ______ a letter when the doorbell rang.
explanation: A longer action in progress interrupted by a shorter past action takes the past continuous.

subject: English
q: While I ______ the road, I saw an accident.
explanation: ‘While’ introducing an action in progress in the past takes the past continuous.

subject: English
q: She ______ to the radio when I phoned her.
explanation: An action in progress at the time of another past action takes the past continuous.

subject: English
q: We ______ in Muzaffarabad when the 2005 earthquake struck.
explanation: A background situation in progress when a sudden past event occurred takes the past continuous.

subject: English
q: I ______ what you mean, but I do not agree.
explanation: Stative verbs such as ‘understand’ are not normally used in the continuous.

subject: English
q: My father ______ this land since 1985.
explanation: ‘Own’ is a stative verb, so the simple present perfect (not the continuous) is used for a state lasting since a past point.

subject: English
q: This biryani ______ delicious.
explanation: ‘Taste’ describing a quality is stative and takes the simple present.

subject: English
q: I ______ the answer now; the teacher explained it.
explanation: ‘Know’ is a stative verb and is not used in the continuous.

subject: English
q: Hurry up! The bus ______.
explanation: An action in progress now is expressed with the present continuous.

subject: English
q: Light ______ faster than sound.
explanation: Universal truths and scientific facts take the simple present.

subject: English
q: Every morning my father ______ the newspaper before breakfast.
explanation: Habitual actions take the simple present.

subject: English
q: According to the schedule, the conference ______ at 10 a.m. tomorrow.
explanation: Timetabled future events are often expressed with the simple present.

subject: English
q: The examination ______ at nine sharp tomorrow, so don’t be late.
explanation: An officially scheduled future event can take the simple present.

subject: English
q: He usually ______ tea, but today he ______ coffee.
explanation: A habit takes the simple present, while a temporary action happening now takes the present continuous.

subject: English
q: When I was young, I ______ swim in the canal every summer.
explanation: ‘Used to’ plus the base form expresses a past habit that no longer continues.

subject: English
q: After ten years in the army, he ______ getting up early.
explanation: ‘Be used to’ plus a gerund means ‘be accustomed to’, unlike ‘used to’ plus an infinitive.

subject: English
q: He ______ smoking last year and feels much healthier now.
explanation: A completed action at a finished past time (last year) takes the simple past.

subject: English
q: The 1965 war ______ for seventeen days.
explanation: A completed event in the past takes the simple past.

subject: English
q: The moment she ______ the news, she burst into tears.
explanation: Two past actions in immediate succession take the simple past.

subject: English
q: This time tomorrow I ______ to Karachi.
explanation: An action that will be in progress at a particular future moment takes the future continuous.

subject: English
q: Don’t phone at eight; we ______ dinner then.
explanation: An activity in progress at a stated future time takes the future continuous.

subject: English
q: Look at those dark clouds! It ______.
explanation: ‘Be going to’ is used for a prediction based on present evidence.

subject: English
q: I ______ you a postcard as soon as I get to London.
explanation: ‘Will’ expresses a promise or future intention in the main clause.

subject: English
q: By next June, she ______ her degree.
explanation: ‘By’ plus a future time shows an action finished before then, requiring the future perfect.

subject: English
q: The engineers say that by 2030 the dam ______.
explanation: A future action finished before a stated time takes the future perfect; since the dam is completed by others, the passive is needed.

subject: English
q: By the time you read this letter, I ______ Pakistan.
explanation: An action that will be completed before another future moment takes the future perfect.

subject: English
q: The chairman has promised that the committee ______ its decision by Friday.
explanation: Completion before a future deadline (by Friday) takes the future perfect.

subject: English
q: Next month my parents ______ married for twenty-five years.
explanation: A state that will have lasted a given length of time at a future point takes the future perfect.

subject: English
q: By the end of this year, I ______ in this department for a decade.
explanation: The duration of an activity up to a future point is expressed by the future perfect continuous.

subject: English
q: I will phone you when I ______ home.
explanation: In time clauses referring to the future, the simple present is used, not ‘will’.

subject: English
q: As soon as the chief guest ______, we will start the ceremony.
explanation: After ‘as soon as’ with future meaning, the simple present is used.

subject: English
q: I will wait here until he ______ from the office.
explanation: After ‘until’ referring to the future, the simple present is used.

subject: English
q: Once the rain ______, we will resume the match.
explanation: After ‘once’ in a future sense, the simple present replaces ‘will’.

subject: English
q: Please switch off the lights before you ______ the office.
explanation: After ‘before’ in a future sense, the simple present is used.

subject: English
q: If you heat ice, it ______.
explanation: A zero conditional (general truth) uses the simple present in both clauses.

subject: English
q: If it rains tomorrow, we ______ the match.
explanation: A first conditional (real future possibility) uses the simple present in the if-clause and ‘will’ in the main clause.

subject: English
q: If I ______ time tomorrow, I will visit you.
explanation: In a first conditional the if-clause takes the simple present, not ‘will’.

subject: English
q: If you do not hurry, you ______ the bus.
explanation: A real future condition takes ‘will’ in the main clause.

subject: English
q: Should you need any help, ______ me at once.
explanation: An inverted ‘should’ conditional refers to a possible future event, and the main clause is often an imperative.

subject: English
q: Suppose it ______ tomorrow, where will we hold the wedding?
explanation: With a real future possibility (‘will we hold’), ‘suppose’ is followed by the simple present.

subject: English
q: If I were you, I ______ the offer.
explanation: The second conditional (unreal present) takes ‘would’ plus the base form in the main clause.

subject: English
q: If I ______ a bird, I would fly over the mountains.
explanation: In an unreal present condition, ‘were’ is used for all persons.

subject: English
q: Were he here now, he ______ us solve this problem.
explanation: An inverted ‘were’ conditional is an unreal present condition and takes ‘would’ in the main clause.

subject: English
q: Supposing he ______ your offer, what would you do?
explanation: With ‘would’ in the main clause, ‘supposing’ is followed by the past tense for a hypothetical situation.

subject: English
q: If she had worked harder, she ______ the examination.
explanation: The third conditional (unreal past) takes ‘would have’ plus the past participle in the main clause.

subject: English
q: Had I known his address, I ______ to him.
explanation: An inverted ‘had’ conditional refers to the unreal past and takes ‘would have’ plus the past participle.

subject: English
q: If you had told me earlier, I ______ you.
explanation: An unreal past condition takes a modal perfect (could/would have + past participle).

subject: English
q: If I had accepted that job, I ______ in Dubai now.
explanation: A mixed conditional links an unreal past condition to a present result, so ‘would be’ is used with ‘now’.

subject: English
q: If she ______ the early train, she would be here by now.
explanation: In a mixed conditional the unreal past condition takes the past perfect.

subject: English
q: I wish I ______ a car of my own.
explanation: ‘Wish’ about a present situation is followed by the past tense.

subject: English
q: Now I wish I ______ harder at school.
explanation: A regret about the past after ‘wish’ takes the past perfect.

subject: English
q: It is high time we ______ the problem of load-shedding seriously.
explanation: ‘It is high time’ is followed by the past tense with present meaning.

subject: English
q: He talks as if he ______ everything.
explanation: After ‘as if’ expressing an unreal present situation, the past tense is used.

subject: English
q: I would rather you ______ now; it is getting dark.
explanation: ‘Would rather’ followed by another subject takes the past tense with present or future meaning.

subject: English
q: I’d rather you ______ anyone about our plans.
explanation: After ‘would rather’ with a different subject, the past tense is used, here in the negative.

subject: English
q: The doctor suggested that he ______ sugar completely.
explanation: After ‘suggest that’, the subjunctive (base form, or ‘should’ + base form) is used.

subject: English
q: He said that he ______ too tired to continue.
explanation: When the reporting verb is in the past, the verb in the reported clause normally moves into the past.

subject: English
q: Our teacher told us that the earth ______ round the sun.
explanation: A universal truth keeps the present tense even after a past reporting verb.

subject: English
q: She told me that she ______ the film the week before.
explanation: A past action reported after a past reporting verb shifts back to the past perfect.

subject: English
q: I didn’t know that you ______ a sister.
explanation: After a past main verb, the subordinate clause normally takes a past tense.

subject: English
q: She promised that she ______ the book the next day.
explanation: A future idea reported after a past verb uses ‘would’ instead of ‘will’.

subject: English
q: He worked day and night so that he ______ pass the examination.
explanation: After a past main verb, a purpose clause with ‘so that’ takes ‘might/could’, not ‘may/can’.

subject: English
q: She works hard so that she ______ win a scholarship.
explanation: After a present main verb, a purpose clause with ‘so that’ takes ‘may/can’.

subject: English
q: I have known him ______ ten years.
explanation: ‘For’ is used with a length of time; ‘since’ with a starting point.

subject: English
q: He has been unwell ______ last Friday.
explanation: ‘Since’ is used with a point in time from which an action has continued.

subject: English
q: The family ______ in this house since 2018.
explanation: A present situation that began at a past point marked by ‘since’ takes the present perfect, not the present tense.

subject: English
q: He worked in Saudi Arabia ______ five years and then returned home.
explanation: A completed period of time in the past takes ‘for’; ‘since’ needs a starting point.

subject: English
q: A great deal has changed since the motorway ______.
explanation: The ‘since’ clause naming the starting point takes the simple past, while the main clause takes the present perfect.

subject: English
q: She ______ to Islamabad three years ago.
explanation: ‘Ago’ refers to a finished past time and takes the simple past.

subject: English
q: ______ he was running a high fever, he attended the meeting.
explanation: ‘Although’ introduces a full clause of contrast; ‘despite’ and ‘in spite of’ need a noun or gerund.

subject: English
q: ______ his illness, he attended the meeting.
explanation: ‘Despite’ is a preposition followed by a noun phrase; ‘although’ and ‘though’ need a clause.

subject: English
q: In spite ______ being tired, she completed the report before leaving.
explanation: The phrase is ‘in spite of’, followed by a noun or gerund.

subject: English
q: Though he is poor, ______ he never compromises on his principles.
explanation: In traditional usage ‘though’ may be paired with ‘yet’, never with ‘but’.

subject: English
q: She continued to work ______ she was exhausted.
explanation: ‘Even though’ introduces a clause of strong contrast; the other options must be followed by a noun.

subject: English
q: Ali prefers cricket, ______ his brother is passionate about hockey.
explanation: ‘Whereas’ contrasts two facts.

subject: English
q: I will not lend him money again ______ he begs me.
explanation: ‘Even if’ means ‘whether or not this happens’.

subject: English
q: The plan was sound; ______, it failed for lack of funds.
explanation: ‘However’ introduces a contrast between two sentences.

subject: English
q: ______ the objections of the opposition, the bill was passed.
explanation: ‘Notwithstanding’ is a preposition meaning ‘in spite of’ and can take a noun phrase; the others need a clause or stand alone.

subject: English
q: You will not pass ______ you work harder.
explanation: ‘Unless’ means ‘if … not’.

subject: English
q: Unless you ______ now, you will miss the flight.
explanation: ‘Unless’ already means ‘if not’, so it is not followed by a negative, and the clause takes the present for future meaning.
